questions.problem: Which curve is defined by the equation $4{x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}=10?$
questions.worked_solution:
Consider the quadratic form $Q(x)=4{x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}.$ To determine the curve defined by the given equation, we reduce $Q(x)$ to its canonical (diagonal) form. 

First, we write down the matrix of $Q(x),$ which is

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Next, we find the eigenvalues of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}4-\lambda  & 2 \\ 2 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-5\lambda  & =0 \\ \lambda  & =5,\,0\end{aligned}
$$

So, our quadratic form can be reduced to $5{y}_{1}^{2}.$ 

In the new variables, the given curve has the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}5{y}_{1}^{2} & =10 \\ {y}_{1}^{2} & =2\end{aligned}
$$

This represents the two parallel lines ${y}_{1}=\sqrt{2}$ and ${y}_{1}=-\sqrt{2}.$

questions.problem: Which curve is defined by the equation $24{x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+21{x}_{2}^{2}=100?$
questions.worked_solution:
Consider the quadratic form $Q(x)=24{x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+21{x}_{2}^{2}.$ To determine the curve defined by the given equation, we reduce $Q(x)$ to its canonical (diagonal) form.  

First, we write down the matrix of $Q(x),$ which is

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}24 & 2 \\ 2 & 21\end{aligned}].
$$

Next, we find the eigenvalues of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}24-\lambda  & 2 \\ 2 & 21-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-45\lambda +500 & =0 \\ \lambda  & =25,\,20\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, our quadratic form can be reduced to $25{y}_{1}^{2}+20{y}_{2}^{2}.$  

In the new variables, the curve has the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}25{y}_{1}^{2}+20{y}_{2}^{2} & =100 \\ \frac{{y}_{1}^{2}}{4}+\frac{{y}_{2}^{2}}{5} & =1 \\ \frac{{y}_{1}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{{y}_{2}^{2}}{(\sqrt{5})^{2}} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes   $2$ and $\sqrt{5}.$

Which of the following diagrams depicts the lines representing the principal axes of the quadratic curve shown above?
questions.worked_solution:
The principal axes of a curve define a coordinate system in which the curve can be represented by its (simplest) canonical equation. 

Our curve is an ellipse. This curve will have the canonical equation of the form

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=1
$$

if the axes pass through the opposite vertices of the ellipse.

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Principal Axes of a Quadratic Plane Curve
questions.problem: Find the principal axes of the curve $7{x}_{1}^{2}-4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+7{x}_{2}^{2}=1.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, consider the quadratic form $Q(x)=7{x}_{1}^{2}-4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+7{x}_{2}^{2}.$ The matrix of the form is

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}7 & -2 \\ -2 & 7\end{aligned}].
$$

Notice that $A$ is symmetric. The principal axes of the curve 

$$
{x}^{T}\,Ax=1
$$

are the vectors that form an orthonormal eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

By solving the characteristic equation $|A-\lambda I|=0,$ we obtain

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=9\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{2}=5.$

Let's now find the eigenvectors.

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=9,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-9I & =[\begin{aligned}7 & -2 \\ -2 & 7\end{aligned}]-9[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 & -2 \\ -2 & -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-9I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=5,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-5I & =[\begin{aligned}7 & -2 \\ -2 & 7\end{aligned}]-5[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-5I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the principal axes of our curve are

$\,$ $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

questions.problem: Consider the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}4 & 3 \\ 3 & -4\end{aligned}]$ and the quadratic curve ${x}^{T}\,Ax=11.$ Given that $A$ has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=5$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-5,$ find the principal axes of the curve.
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that $A$ is symmetric. 
The principal axes of the curve 

$$
{x}^{T}\,Ax=11
$$

are the vectors that give an orthonormal eigenvector basis for $A.$ Let's now find these eigenvectors.

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=5,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-5I & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 3 \\ 3 & -4\end{aligned}]-5[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 \\ 3 & -9\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-5I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{10},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-5,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-5)I & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 3 \\ 3 & -4\end{aligned}]+5[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}9 & 3 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-5)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{10},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the principal axes of our curve are

$\,$ $\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$
